run.question:
1. List the tables in the database and tell me the verification code from the holmes_eval_222 table
2. I'm experiencing slow queries with this SQL: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345
   Analyze why this query is slow and suggest how to fix it

report.summary: Database inventory: the configured ClickHouse target exposes exactly two tables in schema `default` — `orders` and `holmes_eval_222`. The requested verification code is in `holmes_eval_222`, the only row returned: id=1, category=eval_test, verification_code=HOLMES-CLICKHOUSE-EVAL-222-v5t8n2, created_at 2026-11-21 08:41:08 (fact). Slow-query analysis: `orders` is a MergeTree table whose sorting key and primary key are `id` only, with no partition key, holding 10,000 rows in a single part (all_1_1_0, 142,764 bytes on disk) (fact). `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` for the reported SQL shows the primary-key index contributes no condition at all — `Condition: true`, Granules 1/1 — whereas the same EXPLAIN for `id = 42` shows `Condition: (id in [42, 42])`, so the `customer_id` predicate gets no index-based granule pruning and every row must be read (fact). The value in the reported SQL matches nothing: `customer_id` ranges 1..1000 in this data and `WHERE customer_id = 12345` returned 0 rows (fact). On this instance no slow execution was observed: all 47 finished statements recorded in `system.query_log` between 2026-11-21 08:41:08 and 08:41:37 completed in ≤11 ms (max 11 ms, p95 6 ms), and none exceeded 50 ms (fact/counter-evidence). The supported structural explanation is therefore a hypothesis, not an observed latency regression: the missing index/ordering key on `customer_id` makes the predicate a full scan whose cost grows linearly with table size, and `SELECT *` widens the columns read. There is no latency baseline for this table, so no trend is claimed.

claims.text: The configured ClickHouse database lists exactly two tables, both in schema `default`: `holmes_eval_222` (type table) and `orders` (type table).
Table `default.holmes_eval_222` has columns id (UInt32), category (String), verification_code (String), created_at (DateTime, default now()); its primary/sorting key is `id`.
Querying `holmes_eval_222` returned a single row: id=1, category=eval_test, verification_code=HOLMES-CLICKHOUSE-EVAL-222-v5t8n2, created_at=2026-11-21 08:41:08.

Table `default.orders` has columns id (UInt32), customer_id (UInt32), order_date (Date), total_amount (Decimal(10,2)), status (String); the only index reported is a primary/sorting key on `id`, with no index on `customer_id`.

`system.tables` reports `default.orders` as engine MergeTree with sorting_key=id, primary_key=id, empty partition_key, empty sampling_key and total_rows=10000; `system.parts` shows one part named all_1_1_0 in partition tuple() with 10000 rows, 142764 bytes_on_disk and 2 marks.
`orders` holds 10000 rows spanning order_date 2025-11-22 to 2026-11-21 with 1000 distinct customer_id values, and customer_id ranges from 1 to 1000 (min 1, max 1000).
The reported predicate matches no data on this instance: `SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345` returned 0.

`EXPLAIN indexes = 1 SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345` shows ReadFromMergeTree (default.orders) with PrimaryKey `Condition: true`, Parts: 1/1 and Granules: 1/1 — i.e. the primary-key index supplies no readable key condition for this predicate; the same EXPLAIN for `WHERE id = 42` instead shows `Keys: id` and `Condition: (id in [42, 42])`.

Statements against `orders` read the whole table: the count/filter statement on customer_id was recorded in `system.query_log` as QueryFinish with read_rows=10000 and read_bytes=40000 for result_rows=1.

No slow execution was observed on this instance: `system.query_log` contains 47 QueryFinish rows between 2026-11-21 08:41:08 and 08:41:37 with max query_duration_ms=11 and p95=6 ms, and a query for QueryFinish rows with query_duration_ms > 50 returned nothing (status no_data, so absence there is not itself citable).

The most likely cause of slowness for `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345` is the table design: `orders` is ordered/primary-keyed by `id` only, so a filter on `customer_id` cannot prune any granule and ClickHouse must read every row of every part; the cost therefore scales linearly with table size, which is what would make the same statement slow on a larger production table (only 10,000 rows / 142,764 bytes on this instance).

`SELECT *` contributes additional I/O: the projection reads all five columns (id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount, status) for every scanned row instead of only the columns the caller needs, so widening the table schema would increase per-row read volume further. Only the structural projection is evidenced here; no per-column byte measurement was taken.

If the application really sends the literal `customer_id = 12345`, the returned result is empty (customer_id only spans 1..1000), so the observed slowness cannot be explained by a large result set being transferred; a client that retries or polls this empty query could instead amplify perceived latency. This is not verified — no client of this table was observed.

Rejected for this instance: that the query is slow because the table or result set is large. `orders` is a single 10,000-row part (142,764 bytes on disk) and the predicate matches 0 rows, and every statement recorded in the sampled query_log finished within 11 ms.

Make `customer_id` searchable: either add a data-skipping index on `customer_id` (e.g. a minmax or set/bloom_filter skip index) or rebuild the table with `ORDER BY (customer_id, id)` / a projection ordered by customer_id, then verify with `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` that the PrimaryKey/ Skip condition prunes granules instead of showing `Condition: true`.

Avoid `SELECT *` in the application path: list only the required columns, add `ORDER BY order_date DESC LIMIT n` when paging, and pass a customer_id value that exists (the current literal 12345 matches no row in this dataset).

Capture the evidence that is missing before acting on production: run `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` and read `system.query_log` (query_duration_ms, read_rows, read_bytes) for the actual slow statement on the production-sized table, and compare against a baseline, since no slow execution or latency baseline exists on this instance.

gaps: No slow query was observed on this target: `system.query_log` only retains rows from 2026-11-21 08:41:08 to 08:41:37 (this Run's own statements), with max query_duration_ms=11; the production slow execution and its plan are not in the sampled log, so the latency claim itself is unverified.
There is no latency baseline (before/after, or a comparable period) for `orders`, so no latency trend or regression can be stated.

The query `SELECT name, type, expr, granularity FROM system.data_skipping_indices WHERE database='default' AND table='orders'` returned status no_data (0 rows), which is not citable as proof of absence; secondary index coverage of `orders` is therefore unconfirmed beyond the single sorting/primary key on `id` reported by describe-table.
`SHOW CREATE TABLE default.orders` was refused (QUERY_CONSTRUCT_NOT_ALLOWED), so the full DDL, table settings (e.g. index_granularity) and any merge/compaction configuration could not be read.

No client of the `orders` table was identified: no application traces, service metrics or pod logs were tied to these SQL statements, so it is unknown whether the reported slowness comes from an application, an ad-hoc client, or from a different (larger) deployment than this 10,000-row instance.
The size, partitioning and row counts of the production `orders` table are unknown; conclusions about scan cost at scale rest on the schema, not on measured production volume.
The change_history integration is not available in this Run, so it could not be checked whether the table schema or indexes changed before the reported slowness.
next_steps: On the affected production instance, run `EXPLAIN indexes = 1 SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = <value>` and inspect `system.query_log` for that statement's query_duration_ms, read_rows and read_bytes to confirm the full-scan hypothesis at real data volume.

Decide between a data-skipping index on `customer_id` (online, `ALTER TABLE ... ADD INDEX`) and a new table/projection with `ORDER BY (customer_id, id)` (requires backfill), then re-measure the same statement against a captured baseline.
Check whether the calling application needs all five columns and whether it pages results; if it only needs recent orders, add a date predicate on order_date to enable partition/ordering pruning.
Confirm the intended customer_id value with the caller — 12345 does not exist in this dataset (range 1..1000) — so the test reflects a query that returns data.
